We examine finite-time thermodynamic protocols for a quantum harmonic oscillator, focusing on the trade-off between work expenditure and heat dissipation. By applying principles of thermodynamic information geometry, we demonstrate that the protocols achieving minimal work expenditure are characterized by the constant curvature of the geometry of the space of probability distributions. This observation supports a generalized version of the Min-Peierls principle.

This study examines the discovery potential for the vector-like top partner ($T$) at a future 100 TeV proton-proton collider, utilizing the POWHEG framework to incorporate beamstrahlung and initial-state radiation effects. We analyze the impact of these factors on the $T$ production cross-section and subsequent decay into a top quark and a $b$-quark jet, evaluating how they influence the $T$-quark search sensitivity. Our findings indicate that accounting for initial-state radiation and beamstrahlung significantly reduces the $T$-quark search reach. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the $T$-quark search reaches a saturation point when the effective center-of-mass energy distribution is utilized.

Acoustofluidic systems are increasingly utilized to manipulate and analyze biological and chemical agents, yet their fundamental operating principles remain incompletely understood. This study investigates the dynamics of fluid redistribution in a two-dimensional acoustic trap driven by a single, focused acoustic source. We demonstrate that the critical acoustic energy density required to trigger fluid repositioning decreases as channel height increases. Furthermore, we quantify the maximum flow rate within the channel and the associated pressure drop across it. Our findings indicate that the critical energy density scales inversely with the square of the channel height, while both the peak fluid velocity and the pressure drop exhibit a linear dependence on channel height.

This paper investigates the relationship between a Hilbert space multiplication operator and a corresponding, uniquely defined, weighted shift operator on a semi-tree that is either generalized or specifically directed. We establish a correspondence that allows for the transfer of properties from one operator to the other. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the product measure of two probability spaces can be uniquely represented as a weighted shift on an appropriate directed semi-tree.

This study investigates the production of positrons through laser high-intensity interactions with high-Z targets, focusing on how the properties of ultra-short laser pulses influence the resulting energy spectra and angular distributions of positron populations. The analysis utilizes the Quantum Electrodynamics (QEDP) module within the particle-in-cell (PIC) code, which incorporates the QED module. The results indicate that positrons generated from pulses with durations of 100 fs exhibit significantly higher energies and a forward-peaked angular distribution compared to those produced by pulses lasting 10 fs.

Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) have proven highly effective for event prediction, yet their inherent limitation lies in the indiscriminate aggregation of graph information, which often results in irrelevant data being included in the final predictions. To address this, we introduce a new gating mechanism designed to enhance the GCNN's ability to filter graph data. This approach utilizes a specialized gating function that selectively regulates the contribution of graph features during the message-passing phase. By learning to distinguish between pertinent and irrelevant information, the model ensures that only significant data is utilized for forecasting. Empirical results demonstrate that this proposed gating mechanism consistently surpasses baseline GCNN models across various event prediction tasks.

This study examines the impact of Gaussian noise in both features and responses within Bayesian linear regression. We introduce a novel, computationally efficient variational Bayes method for the Gaussian linear regression model with heteroscedastic errors. This method is designed to be robust against misspecification of the prior. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the variational posterior mean converges to the true parameters at a linear rate. Finally, we validate our findings through simulation experiments and a real-world data analysis.

Quantum many-body systems are frequently employed to investigate complex phenomena, including entanglement. However, the physical parameters defining these models are often uncertain, which can significantly hinder the actualization of targeted quantum states. This study examines how such parameter uncertainty influences the entanglement of many-body systems, specifically within the context of the transverse-field Ising model. We demonstrate that the impact of this uncertainty can be precisely quantified by analyzing the fidelity between the desired and the experimentally realized states. Furthermore, we evaluate the sensitivity of this fidelity to variations in physical parameters across different experimental protocols, including global quenches, local quenches, and quenching to a thermal state.

This study introduces a framework for estimating the Jacobian of nonlinear systems using noisy data. By leveraging a variant of the shift-invert Arnoldi method, we construct a model that offers more precise estimates than traditional Arnoldi approaches. The shift-invert variant prioritizes the eigenvalues closest to a specific shift parameter, which can be strategically selected to align with the spectral characteristics of the Jacobian. Furthermore, we examine the impact of noise on this estimation technique and demonstrate its application in a fluid dynamics context.

This study examines a semilinear transport equation featuring a time-dependent absorption coefficient. We demonstrate that the absorption coefficient can be recovered from a solution by leveraging its total variation. Specifically, we consider the Cauchy problem for the equation $u_t + u_x = u^2$ with a time-dependent absorption coefficient $a(t)$ and initial data $u(x,0) = h(x)$. Assuming the solution is uniquely determined by the absorption coefficient and the initial data, we show that the absorption coefficient can be recovered from the solution at a fixed point $x_0$.

Explainable reinforcement learning (XRL) is a rapidly evolving domain that has garnered significant interest from both the machine learning and reinforcement learning communities. This survey aims to provide a comprehensive overview of XRL by addressing three key areas: (1) defining the scope of XRL and its significance; (2) categorizing existing literature into four distinct groups; and (3) highlighting promising avenues for future research. Specifically, the first section outlines the fundamental challenges of XRL and proposes a taxonomy for the identified methods and applications. The second section classifies the existing body of work into four categories: (i) explanation methods for model-free reinforcement learning, (ii) approaches for model-based RL, (iii) techniques for offline RL, and (iii) methods for continuous action spaces. Finally, the paper concludes by identifying critical open problems, including the development of standardized evaluation metrics, the creation of benchmark datasets, and the formulation of unified taxonomies for future inquiry.

This work examines the axiomatization of first-order lattice-valued logics through the lens of dual algebraic semantics. By applying a dualization strategy, we utilize functional representation theorems to derive a general, complete axiomatization for a specific class of these logics. This framework is applicable to numerous examples, including the modal logic of subspaces and the logic of subspaces and relations.

This work examines the expected signature of a fractional Brownian motion with Hurst parameter $H$ within the range $[0, 1/2]$ and extends beyond to $H \in (0, 1)$. For any $H > 1/4$, the expected signature is found to be a convex combination of the Brownian motion signature and the fractional Brownian motion signatures corresponding to $H = 1/2$.

This study examines the performance of a localization system in millimeter-wave (mmWave) networks, specifically focusing on the impact of node placement strategies. The proposed system utilizes a single reference node and a mobile target node, where localization is achieved through Time-of-Arrival (ToA) measurements of mmWave signals. The research analyzes how the spatial distribution of both the reference and target nodes influences localization accuracy. To evaluate the system's performance, the Cramér-Rao Lower Bound (CRLB) is derived for the ToA-based localization approach. The analysis demonstrates that the CRLB is contingent upon the node distributions and can be modeled as a function of the spatial densities of the reference and target nodes. Furthermore, the CRLB is utilized to compare two specific node placement schemes: the Random Waypoint (RWP) model and a Poisson Point Process (PPP). The findings reveal that the CRLB under RWP is generally lower than that under PPP, indicating superior localization performance with the RWP strategy. Additionally, the CRLB is evaluated under various conditions, including different node densities, target node densities, and varying transmission powers.

We examine the behavior of trapped Bose gases under the influence of weak interaction potentials, which can be modeled using a series of discrete two-body states. By analyzing the system's grand potential within the canonical ensemble, we derive expressions for thermodynamic quantities such as the mean occupation of two-body states and the chemical potential. Our analysis reveals that interaction-induced modifications to the condensate fraction and chemical potential are governed by a single dimensionless parameter, which we utilize to categorize the system into three distinct regimes: one dominated by the ideal gas limit, another characterized by mean-field effects, and a third where interactions are strong.

This study introduces a novel deep learning framework for image inpainting, which reconstructs missing regions by synthesizing semantic structures and textural details. Our proposed method employs a dual-stage architecture: the initial stage restores the global structure of the input image, while the subsequent stage generates fine-grained textures by leveraging a pre-trained convolutional neural network. Specifically, this stage utilizes the network's learned filters to capture texture characteristics, which are then modulated by the semantic information of the reconstructed stage to produce a high-fidelity inpainting result. Extensive experiments on the MS-COCO dataset demonstrate that the method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques, achieving superior scores in both structural (SSIM) and perceptual (PSNR) metrics.

This study examines the Thresholding Bandit problem, a scenario where the primary goal is to identify all items with a value exceeding a specific but unknown threshold. We demonstrate that the problem's probability of error can be decomposed into two distinct components: one stemming from the necessity of arm sampling and the other from the decision-making process itself. Leveraging this decomposition, we establish both lower and upper bounds on the sample complexity for various configurations of arm count ($K$), target items ($L$), and confidence levels ($\delta$). Furthermore, we introduce a novel algorithm that achieves an optimal sample complexity for every such configuration.

We explore the application of proof compression in establishing the equivalence of NP with co-NP, as well as other major complexity class relationships like P vs. NP, NP hierarchy, and BPP. By utilizing Tseitin formulas, we demonstrate that NP can prove statements of the form "there exists a satisfying assignment for the Tseitin formula on a given graph." Furthermore, we show that NP can prove these same statements using significantly shorter proofs than the standard polynomial time upper bound allows. This proof compression enables us to derive the conclusion that NP = co-NP.

This study examines the mean curvature flow of a broad category of hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ that are strictly mean convex and possess a small $L^n$ norm. The analysis demonstrates that, in dimensions $n \geq 3$, this class of hypersurfaces exhibits a stability property analogous to that of small convex hypersurfaces. Furthermore, we establish that the corresponding solutions remain defined for all time and asymptotically converge to the Euclidean sphere after a suitable rescaling.

This study investigates the vortex-vortex distribution function within the framework of the two-dimensional XY model, utilizing Monte Carlo simulations. The results indicate that the separation between vortices follows an exponential decay at low temperatures but transitions to power-law decay at high temperatures. The extracted critical temperature aligns well with the value predicted by Kosterlitz and others.

Public sentiment regarding artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly intensifying, significantly influencing the technology's adoption and regulatory framework. This paper introduces a novel framework designed to analyze public opinion within a specific domain by leveraging the latent semantic structure of online discourse. We propose a two-stage Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) model that utilizes a "topic-embedding" mechanism to capture the interconnections among distinct topics. This approach is applied to a comprehensive collection of 1.5 million articles from 1,000 news outlets, focusing specifically on AI news. By employing topic-embedding space analysis, we visualize the relationships between topics and identify a central cluster of subjects that define the current AI discourse. Furthermore, we utilize LDA-based topic modeling to examine the temporal evolution of these core topics, revealing that the proportion of positive sentiment toward AI has been declining over time.

This study presents the initial measurement of the branching fraction for the $\Xi_c^0$ baryon decaying into a $\pi^-$ and a $\Lambda_c^+$ baryon. Utilizing data from $3.0\,\text{fb}^{-1}$ of proton-proton collisions collected by the LHCb detector at a center-of-mass energy of $7\,\text{TeV}$, the analysis identifies $\Xi_c^0$ decays through the $\Lambda_c^+\pi^-$ intermediate state. The measured branching fraction is determined to be $(1.19\pm0.10\pm0.14)\times10^{-3}$, where the first uncertainty is statistical and the second is systematic.

This study introduces an approximation technique for resolving hybrid nonlinear equations. The authors establish convergence theorems regarding iterative sequences and apply these findings to hybrid nonlinear equations within fixed point theory. Additionally, a numerical example is provided to support the derived theorems.

Safety is a critical concern in reinforcement learning (RL), particularly when deploying learned policies in the real world. While recent studies have introduced various techniques to mitigate safety constraint violations, they often fail to account for the impact of safety on reward. This paper introduces a new method that integrates safety considerations directly into the reward function, thereby reducing safety breaches. Our approach involves a two-step process: first, we employ a neural network to estimate the probability of safety constraint violations; second, we utilize this probability to adjust the reward. Experiments across diverse RL environments demonstrate that our method significantly lowers the likelihood of safety breaches while maintaining high returns.

This study examines the superradiant phase transition within a cavity QED framework, where the interaction between cavity photons and an ensemble of two-level atoms is mediated by a Kerr nonlinearity. We identify a chiral superradiant phase characterized by a non-zero photon current circulating around the cavity perimeter, a phenomenon that distinguishes itself from conventional superradiant states by exhibiting a distinct phase diagram. Furthermore, the current's directionality is tunable via external control of the atomic configuration. We also pinpoint a region in the phase diagram where cavity photons form a vortex state, defined by a phase gradient proportional to the radial distance from the center. Finally, we demonstrate that the proposed model can generate a topological superfluid, where the circuit current remains robust against perturbations.

This paper introduces a decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning framework utilizing a hierarchical, adaption-based Transformer architecture. By leveraging the hierarchical structure of the QTransformer, the system enhances coordination among agents. Furthermore, the level-adaptive mechanism allows the Q-value estimates of individual agents to function as contextual inputs, dynamically adjusting the model's capacity based on the predicted value levels of those agents. This design enables the Q-Transformer to effectively capture intricate agent interactions and relationships. We evaluate the proposed method on two challenging multi-agent benchmarks: the StarCraft II Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC) and the Multi-Agent Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Challenge (MABM). Empirical results demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques, delivering superior performance across both test environments.

Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has recently gained significant traction within the field of swarm robotics, a domain that has seen substantial growth in recent years. However, this study specifically targets particle robot systems, which are distinct from traditional swarms due to their focus on individual agents rather than collective behavior. While deep RL has proven effective for single robots, its application to these systems remains largely unexplored. This paper addresses the challenge of enabling deep RL agents to navigate within a particle robot framework. We introduce a novel algorithm designed to generate feasible trajectories for these agents, demonstrating its efficacy in solving a specific path-planning task. Furthermore, we validate the algorithm's performance across various scenarios, including path optimization, and evaluate its robustness against perturbations.

The exoplanet WASP-31b, a hot Jupiter with a notably low density, is a prime candidate for studying atmospheric chemistry and dynamics. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of its transmission spectrum, utilizing data from the Hubble Space Telescope's WFC3 instrument across the 0.6–1.6 $\mu$m range. By employing a Bayesian framework that integrates both Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) and Nested Sampling methods, researchers examined a wide array of atmospheric models. These models varied in their treatment of clouds, including scenarios with no clouds, those with a single uniform layer, and those with vertically distributed layers. The results indicate that clouds are essential to explain the observed data; specifically, a single uniform layer of clouds obscures the signatures of water and potassium, while a vertically distributed layer significantly dampens spectral slope variations. Furthermore, the study found that the derived atmospheric metallicity is highly sensitive to the chosen cloud model, with metallicities ranging from 100 to 1000 times solar levels.

This study examines the performance of large-scale, tightly coupled applications within HPC-as-a-Service (HPCaaS) environments. We demonstrate that deploying too many instances in such scenarios can lead to significant performance degradation. Consequently, we propose a framework for selecting optimal cloud configurations, which includes a method for choosing the right number of instances, their placement, and the specific architecture. This framework is validated using a case study of a distributed parameter optimization task. We evaluate the approach against various cloud settings, including private clouds, public clouds, and a hybrid setup. Our results indicate that HPCaaS is best suited for scaling out tightly coupled applications using a limited number of instances, particularly when a hybrid cloud architecture is employed.

This study introduces a new approach to analyzing the functional connectivity (FC) of the human brain by applying graph theory to the latent representations of pairs of fMRI scans. The method begins by deriving FC graphs from the latent representations of two patient scans, which are then compared using a graph edit distance metric. The authors demonstrate that this metric effectively differentiates between heterogeneous and homogeneous patient pairs, a capability that aligns with the distinct clinical characteristics of these groups. Additionally, the research evaluates the metric's sensitivity to variations in graph construction parameters and confirms its robustness against noise. Finally, the authors illustrate that this metric can be utilized to identify patient pairs with the most similar clinical outcomes.

The Milgram Gauss sum formula serves as a valuable instrument for calculating the signature of non-singular forms, particularly when the order is 2. In this paper, we extend this formula to apply to degenerate forms as well.

This study presents experimental data on Cherenkov radiation in the X-ray spectrum, acquired using a 10 GeV electron beam at the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. The observed emission characteristics align closely with theoretical predictions based on a specific transition radiation model. Furthermore, the data reveals a novel class of Cherenkov radiation originating from the vacuum chamber walls, which is attributed to surface roughness.

The human capacity to comprehend language relies on the ability to infer the meaning of words within their context. While most research in natural language processing has prioritized extracting information explicitly stated in text, understanding implicit information—such as arguments for an action that are not directly mentioned—is equally vital for grasping sentence semantics. This work introduces a novel dataset comprising 1,000 sentences, each annotated with up to 10 latent arguments. We demonstrate that these unexplicit details are essential for accurate interpretation and that current state-of-theart models fail to predict them. Additionally, we propose a new architecture capable of learning to infer these missing elements, achieving a 20% improvement over baseline methods on our dataset.

This study introduces a new framework designed to simultaneously localize the lung field and identify pulmonary diseases in chest X-rays. The proposed architecture integrates a novel loss function that enhances localization accuracy by refining confidence scores based on the spatial context of the disease. Additionally, the system employs a specialized attention mechanism to concentrate on diagnostically critical regions. To address the scarcity of annotated data, the authors developed a method for generating synthetic labels from unlabeled datasets. Extensive experiments on the public MIMIC-CXR dataset demonstrate that this approach significantly surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods.

This study introduces a penalized minimum Hellinger distance (PHMD) statistic designed for model selection in small samples. The approach involves applying a penalty term to the HMD statistic, which serves as a dissimilarity metric between observed and theoretical distributions. The penalty term is constructed using a kernel density estimator, which is particularly effective for selecting models when sample sizes are limited. The proposed method demonstrates robust performance in selecting the correct model and maintaining a low rate of false positives. Additionally, it offers a viable solution for model selection in high-dimensional settings. The efficacy of this approach is validated through both simulation experiments and a real-world application.

The Prouhet-Thue-Morse sequence ($\mathbf{t}$) is a non-terminating binary string that lacks both left and right contexts for a finite set of non-overlapping binary strings. Despite this, these patterns appear within $\mathbf{t}$ in a non-trivial manner. We demonstrate that this phenomenon stems from a specific self-similarity property of $\mathbf{t}$, which is linked to the fact that the sequence possesses balanced characteristics.

Cost-sensitive hierarchical clustering (CSHC) involves a set of algorithms where each incurs a specific expense upon application, and the objective is to minimize total expenditure while maintaining a pre-assessed error rate. This framework effectively models key areas such as algorithm selection, multi-objective optimization, and active learning. This paper introduces a novel approach to CSHC that leverages a Bayesian framework to estimate error rates, utilizing a Gaussian process (GP) prior over the input space. The method employs a GPyOpt optimization loop to iteratively query the GP, thereby refining error estimations for a selected subset of algorithms. The process terminates once a satisfactory level of confidence is achieved. The proposed approach is evaluated on active learning and algorithm selection tasks, demonstrating that it can accurately estimate error distributions and identify optimal, cost-efficient configurations.

The 21cm signal from neutral hydrogen is a primary target for cosmological studies, yet it is extremely faint and typically obscured by foregrounds that are orders of magnitude brighter. To isolate the desired signal, researchers employ a technique called foreground removal, which relies on the distinct spectral smoothness of these foregrounds compared to the 21cm signal. This paper introduces a novel approach utilizing convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to separate foregrounds from the 21cm signal. We trained the network using simulated datasets that incorporate realistic foregrounds and radio-frequency interference (RFI). Our results demonstrate that the CNN effectively filters out foregrounds and eliminates RFI while maintaining the integrity of the 21cm signal. Additionally, we validated the CNN's performance on real observational data from the EDGES experiment, confirming its capability to handle actual datasets.

This study investigates the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of the novel two-dimensional materials, $\alpha$-Fe$_2$Se$_3$ and Fe$_2$Se$_3$O, utilizing first-principles calculations. Our findings indicate that both compounds exhibit semiconducting behavior with band gaps of 1.11 eV and 1.13 eV, respectively. Notably, Fe$_2$Se$_3$O demonstrates ferromagnetic properties with a calculated Curie temperature exceeding 300 K, a value that surpasses room temperature. Additionally, we analyzed the magnetic phase diagram of Fe$_2$Se$_3$O, revealing that it remains in a ferromagnetic state under applied magnetic fields exceeding 10 T at temperatures below 100 K.

We present a method for constructing positive definite functions defined on the product of two quasi-metric spaces, given that their individual positive definite functions are known. This method extends the work of the second author, who previously established a similar technique for building positive definite functions on finite Cartesian products of quasi-metric spaces.

The growing prevalence of data-driven research in medicine and public health has heightened the need for robust methods to detect hidden biases in observational studies. This paper introduces a novel approach to identifying such biases by leveraging case description data. By leveraging the intuition that case details are more likely to be recorded when a disease is distinct from its exposure, we propose a model that utilizes these descriptions to estimate the sensitivity of results to concealed confounding. We demonstrate that this approach can be integrated into standard sensitivity analyses, such as those using unmeasured confounding bias factors, to assess how case selection bias impacts these evaluations. Furthermore, we introduce a novel test statistic that quantifies the degree of sensitivity to hidden bias, which can be applied to determine whether a specific study warrants further investigation. We validate this methodology through simulations and a real-world case study involving the link between asthma and air pollution.

We establish a correspondence between the Chow groups of 0-cycles and Suslin homology for a project scheme that is normal, extending earlier findings by R. Kahn and M. Levine. This generalization relies on a theorem by A. Suslin concerning the Chow groups of 0-cycles with coefficients in twisted coefficient rings. Furthermore, we demonstrate an isomorphism between the Chow groups of 0-cycles and Suslin homology for a smooth projective scheme $X$ over a field $k$, provided that the torsion prime-to-the characteristic components of $H^i(X)$ vanish for all $i \leq 2\dim X$.

This study presents measurements of the $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$ production cross-sections in proton-proton collisions occurring at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The analysis focuses on $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$ mesons with transverse momenta ($p_{\rm T}$) ranging from 0 to 10 GeV/$c$ and pseudorapidity ($\eta$) between 2.0 and 4.0, utilizing the LHCb detector. The study examines the dependence of the cross-section on the event multiplicity of charged particles, as well as on the cross-section's correlation with the $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$ transverse momentum. The findings indicate that the mean $p_{\rm T}$ for $\psi(2S)$ mesons increases with higher event multiplicity, while the $J/\psi/\psi(2S)$ production cross-section ratio remains constant across all multiplicity levels. Additionally, the $J/\psi/\psi(2S)$ cross-section ratio exhibits a dependence on $p_{\rm T}$, a trend that is consistent with previous results from the LHCb experiment.

We introduce a novel protocol for determining the entropy of a quantum system, which offers a significant advantage over prior methods by eliminating the necessity for measurements in the energy eigenbasis. Specifically, our approach enables the measurement of spin-1/2 entropy within a thermal state through an average count of only three.
This study applies the Geometric Principle of the Modulus to derive classical results in analytical theory through an unconventional analytical perspective.

This study examines the discrete Schrödinger equation featuring both long-range interactions and nonlinear terms. We demonstrate that the soliton solutions inherent to the standard discrete Schrödinger equation remain stable under this equation, provided the parameter $\alpha$ is sufficiently large.

Signomial programming represents a specific category of geometric programming, distinguished by the requirement that signomials maintain positive signs. This paper introduces a modification of the MM algorithm, a well-established method for solving signomial programming problems, a technique grounded in the majorization principle. The proposed method leverages this principle to construct a surrogate function that is both convex and linear, thereby converting the original constrained optimization challenge into a series of unconstrained ones. The study further demonstrates that the proposed method guarantees convergence to a stationary point. Additionally, a numerical example is provided to validate the method's efficacy.

Although a hyperkähler manifold cannot exhibit Kobayashi hyperbosity, we demonstrate that its affine variety of stable Higgs bundles possesses this hyperbolic property on an open region. This finding has profound implications for the moduli of irreducible local systems on a Riemann surface.

This paper introduces a new framework for generating personalized 3D avatars from sparse depth data. Unlike existing methods that demand exhaustive scans or extensive multi-view imagery, our approach successfully creates detailed avatars using just a few scattered depth measurements. We achieve this by integrating a multi-scale transformer with a differentiable renderer, enabling the system to infer missing geometry and texture by leveraging both local geometric cues and global structural context. Furthermore, our model is designed to handle missing data and noisy inputs robustly, even when dealing with partial observations. We validate the method's effectiveness on both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its ability to produce high-fidelity, personalized avatars from merely a few depth scans.

Face de-occlusion is a challenging computer vision task that has recently seen significant advancements through the integration of 3D morphable models (3DMMs). However, existing approaches often fail to fully leverage the expressive capabilities of 3DMMs, primarily because they rely on a single 3DMM instance for each target image. This limitation restricts the models' ability to account for variations in facial appearance and identity. To address this, we introduce a new framework that utilizes a set of 3DMMs to enhance de-occlusion performance. Our approach first employs a pre-trained face super-resolution network to generate high-quality facial regions within occluded areas. Subsequently, we propose a 3DMM selection strategy that identifies the most appropriate model from a set of candidates based on the recovered facial features. Finally, we develop a 3DMM adaptation mechanism to refine the selected 3DMM, ensuring it aligns precisely with the visible facial regions in the input. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in both visual quality and metric scores.

The concept of intrinsic motivation has been proposed as a solution to the challenges of exploration and reinforcement learning, offering an alternative to traditional methods. This intrinsic approach relies on the agent's internal representation of its environment to guide exploration and learning, in contrast to classic strategies that depend on external rewards. This study investigates the impact of varying the agent's internal representation on its reinforcement learning capabilities. We introduce a new method for generating exploration policies that utilizes a generative model to assess the agent's current understanding of its environment. This generative model is trained using the agent's past experiences and serves as the foundation for deriving a policy. We demonstrate that the performance of this approach is highly sensitive to the specific generative model employed. Furthermore, we evaluate the proposed method against established exploration strategies and two existing intrinsically motivated methods, showing that it achieves superior performance in certain scenarios.

This study examines a distributed variant of policy iteration designed for multi-agent systems, where agents iteratively refine their policies by exchanging information with immediate neighbors. We demonstrate that the optimality gap of the resulting decentralized policy scales quadratically with the neighborhood size, specifically proportional to the square of this radius. Additionally, we analyze the convergence behavior of a proposed stochastic implementation of this algorithm, proving that the expected rate of optimality gap reduction follows a linear relationship relative to the iteration count.

This study examines the cross sections for events devoid of charged particles in $pp$ collisions at 13 TeV, utilizing the ATLAS detector. The analysis focuses on the inclusive cross section and its differential distribution with respect to transverse momentum ($p_{\mathrm{T}}$), covering the range from 0.2 to 20 GeV. The data are derived from a 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ integrated luminosity sample collected at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The observed results are compared against theoretical predictions derived from next-to-leading order (NLO) calculations incorporating a color-singlet exchange hypothesis, as well as those from a leading-order (LO) simulation including this same exchange. The measured cross sections align well with predictions that explicitly account for color-singlet exchange; conversely, calculations assuming the absence of such exchange significantly underestimate the data.

The electronic band structure of penta-silicene is highly tunable, offering significant promise for applications in spintronics and quantum computing. This study investigates the spin dynamics of penta-silicene by analyzing the spin-dependent electronic bands and spin-orbit coupling (SOC) induced by external electric fields. We demonstrate that SOC can be effectively manipulated through electric field application, a capability that is further enhanced by the material's high dielectric constant. These findings indicate that penta-silizen is an ideal candidate for spintronic devices, where spin polarization can be precisely controlled via electrical gating.

This study examines the thermal dissociation of heavy quarkonium within the fractional framework of the fractional Rutherford atom. The dissociation process is analyzed using the improved Bertrand and Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin (IKIM-BK) methods, which are applied to a fractional Coulomb potential. We demonstrate that the decomposition temperature rises with an increasing fractional parameter. Additionally, we investigate the influence of the principal quantum number ($n$) on the heavy quarkonium's dissociation temperature. Our findings indicate that the fractional heavy quarkonium model exhibits a higher dissociation temperature compared to the conventional quantum mechanical model.

Historical collisions between Earth and dark matter subhalos could have left physical traces in geological materials, potentially including those from the Sun's local environment, known as the local interstellar cloud. This study examines the impact of such encounters on the Sun's outer layers, specifically investigating whether these interactions could have triggered a surge in solar wind that eroded primordial atmospheres from rocky exoplanets orbiting nearby stars. By analyzing the Sun's magnetic field and its interaction with the local interstellar medium, we identify a potential signature of such an event in the form of a "magnetic mirror" effect. This phenomenon would have caused charged particles to be reflected back into space, leading to a significant reduction in the Sun's mass loss rate. By comparing this theoretical magnetic mirror effect with observed data from the Sun's magnetic field and its interaction with the local interstellar medium, we identify a potential signature of such an event in the form of a "magnetic mirror" effect. This phenomenon would have caused charged particles to be reflected back into space, leading to a significant reduction in the Sun's mass loss rate. This study addresses the challenge of coordinating a fleet of autonomous mobile robots to patrol a set of targets. The proposed framework integrates a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) approach with a hierarchical architecture to enhance coordination. The MARL component utilizes a hierarchical graph neural network (HGN) to model the state-action space, while the hierarchical layer facilitates inter-agent communication. To manage the vast state-action space, the hierarchical structure decomposes it into two tiers: the lower level handles immediate actions for individual agents, while the upper level focuses on the collective patrolling of targets. Furthermore, the research incorporates uncertainty into the decision-making process by employing a Bayesian deep Q-network (BDDQN) to generate action distributions that balance exploration and exploitation. The findings demonstrate that this combination of MARL and the hierarchical structure significantly improves patrolling efficiency. Additionally, the integration of uncertainty into the policy yields more robust decision-making capabilities.

This paper introduces a new framework for robot navigation that integrates deep reinforcement learning (DRL) with a graph-based path planner. By leveraging the strengths of both approaches, the method achieves higher success rates and superior trajectory quality compared to prior solutions. Specifically, DRL is employed to refine the path planner's capabilities, ensuring it generates more robust routes in complex environments. Furthermore, the system utilizes a neural network to generate a compact path representation, enabling the robot to reach its goal more efficiently. Experimental results indicate that this approach outperforms existing methods in generating high-quality paths.

This study examines the magnetic phase diagram of a dipole ensemble situated on a face-centered cubic (FCC) lattice. We demonstrate that this system exhibits a complex phase diagram characterized by extensive regions of commensurate phases, which are interspersed with narrow strips of incommensurate phases. The diagram is segmented into three distinct sections based on the magnitude of the dipole moments. Within the low-momentum regime, dipoles align to form a honeycomb structure. In the high-momentum regime, dipoles align to create a body-centered cubic (bcc) structure. These three phases are separated by two transition regions, where dipoles adopt a configuration comprising both honeycomb and bcc sublattices.

This study addresses the challenge of identifying a homogeneous inclusion with constant conductivity within a bounded domain using external measurements. We demonstrate that such an inclusion can be uniquely determined and locally recoverable from Dirichlet-Neumann maps, provided these maps are established on a sufficiently large portion of the boundary. Furthermore, we establish a uniqueness theorem for reconstructing a homogeneous inclusion with piecewise constant conductivity possessing three distinct conductivity values.

Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) is a fundamental operation in scientific computing, yet its performance heavily relies on the specific sparsity pattern of the matrix. To optimize SpMV across diverse hardware, one must determine the most effective data layout, the most efficient execution strategy, and the optimal programming model. This paper presents a unified framework for addressing these three dimensions, leveraging the concept of "tiled execution" to enable a flexible and efficient SpMV implementation. By utilizing a novel data layout, the proposed method achieves a 1.5x speedup on CPUs and a 1.7x speedup on GPUs compared to state-of-the-art solutions. Furthermore, the approach is inherently parallelizable, allowing for seamless scaling across multiple threads and cores.

This study establishes a link between the shared points of two families of meromorphic functions and the normality of one relative to the other. We demonstrate that when two meromorphic families, $\mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{H}$, each share a point partially with $\mathcal{F}$ normal to $\mathcal{H}$ and vice versa, it implies that $\mathcal{H}$ is also normal. Furthermore, we present an example illustrating that this result remains valid even if the condition of partial sharing is altered to allow for a shared point with a different counting multiplicity.

Intention recognition serves as a vital component of human-robot collaboration (HRC), enabling robots to anticipate user goals and execute appropriate actions. While current methods often employ complex, multi-modal approaches that analyze diverse data streams like speech, facial expressions, and gestures, this work proposes a simplified alternative relying exclusively on textual inputs. By utilizing a pre-trained language model, the system processes natural language descriptions of activities to recognize intentions. This strategy enhances the feasibility of HRC in unstructured environments where natural language is more accessible than natural language. Experimental results indicate that this approach achieves comparable performance to existing multi-modal methods, effectively reducing computational complexity and implementation costs.

This study demonstrates that homogeneous Monge-Ampère systems can be characterized by pairs of geometries linked via Lagrangian dualities. We establish the existence of such systems for three specific instances: the projective, hyperbolic, and symplectic geometries. Furthermore, we present a novel geometric framework for defining projective duality, which extends classical concepts by accommodating degenerate conics and points at infinity.

This study examines the natural convection of a dilute electrolyte solution within a horizontal electrolytic cell, where a constant current density is applied to the central plane of the cell. The analysis focuses on the interaction between solutal natural convection and the resulting flow dynamics. The findings indicate that solutal natural convection significantly influences bubble behavior, causing them to detach from the anode surface at a higher rate. Additionally, the magnitude of the cell's average current density is observed to be highly sensitive to variations in electrolyte properties, bubble behavior, and the specific electrolysis mode.

This study examines the potential for discovering supersymmetry in the context of long-lived neutralinos, which decay into a pair of charginos and sleptons within the detector. The analysis focuses on the M2 MSSM scenario, where the lightest neutralino is predominantly composed of the muon-sneutrino. The investigation covers a wide spectrum of proper decay lengths, ranging from $c\tau \sim 1$ mm to $c\tau \sim 100$ m. For shorter lifetimes ($c\tau \lesssim 10$ m), the analysis utilizes the ATLAS detector's impact parameter resolution to identify displaced vertices. Conversely, for longer lifetimes ($c\tau \gtrsim 10$ m), the study employs the ATLAS muon system's detector of isolated, non-pointing muons. The derived exclusion limits on the mass of the lightest neutralino are presented as a function of its proper decay length, and the findings are compared with the standard model predictions.

This study examines the specific heat of Dirac semimetals characterized by anisotropic Fermi surfaces. By employing the Dirac Hamiltonian to model the system, we demonstrate that the specific heat's temperature dependence varies significantly with the extent to which full rotational symmetry is violated. In the scenario where full symmetry is broken, the specific heat's temperature dependence transitions from a linear relationship to a quadratic one as the degree of anisotropy intensifies.

This work introduces a novel methodology for automatically converting sequential code into concurrent Answer Set Programming (ASP) using multi-set sets. The approach involves encoding the ASP program as sequential code and defining an accompanying ASP program that encurses the rules for multi-set set transformation. The results are then compiled into a multi-set set transformation program. The method is demonstrated on several illustrative examples.

We present a novel torsion pendulum setup designed to detect the gravitational pull from objects as light as 1 milligram, with a projected sensitivity of 10^-11 N/m^2. This sensitivity level is sufficient to investigate potential deviations from the inverse-square law at the sub-millimeter scale. The experiment utilizes a Wheatstone bridge configuration to mitigate the torque generated by Earth's tidal forces. Our analysis indicates that the apparatus can identify gravitational attraction down to masses of 1 milligram, corresponding to a minimum detectable change in force of 10^-11 N/m^2.

CCH serves as a valuable probe for detecting polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and their derivatives in the interstellar medium. This study reports the first detection of CCH toward the star-forming region Sgr B2(N), alongside observations of CN, CN, and CN. The CCH abundance ratio relative to these cyanide species is approximately 0.1, which is roughly ten times higher than the corresponding ratios observed in benzene. This elevated ratio suggests that CCH may be abundant in the circumstellar envelope of Sgr B2(N) due to the presence of cyclopentadiene and other five-membered ring structures. Furthermore, the detection of CN in this region indicates that benzene is also present. These findings offer new insights into the chemical processes occurring within the circumstellar envelope of Sgr B2(N).

We propose a unified framework for the origins of asymmetric dark matter and baryogenesis, grounded in a model featuring a dark matter particle and a dark force carrier that interact via a vector boson. This interaction is governed by a $U(1)_D$ symmetry, which is spontaneously broken to generate a massive dark force mediator. We demonstrate that this approach satisfies the requirements for the thermal production of asymmetric dark matter, while simultaneously accounting for baryogenesis. The model incorporates a dark sector $U(1)_D$ symmetry that remains unbroken at the electroweak scale, thereby avoiding the need for additional Higgs fields. Furthermore, we show that this symmetry can be broken at temperatures below those of the QCD phase transition, resulting in dark matter acquiring mass through the QCD scale.

This study presents a measurement of the $t\bar{t}Z$ process cross section using data from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, recorded by the ATLAS detector at the LHC. The analysis utilizes an integrated luminosity of 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ acquired during 2015 and 2016. The $t\bar{t}Z$ events are identified via their final state signatures, which consist of two isolated leptons, missing transverse momentum, and jets originating from $b$-quarks. The observed cross section aligns with Standard Model predictions within a 10% uncertainty margin. Furthermore, the measured differential cross sections for the $t\bar{t}Z$ process demonstrate strong agreement with both Standard Model predictions and theoretical calculations based on next-to-leading-order (NLO) QCD.

This study examines the moduli space of the STU model of $N=2, D=4$ supergravity, specifically focusing on its symplectic Tomonaka group and the associated symplectic orbits. We analyze black hole solutions corresponding to D-term and F-term, demonstrating that their classifications align with semisimple and mixed orbits. Furthermore, we investigate the Higgs branches of the black hole moduli space, which are governed by the Higgs branches of the $U(1)^3$ quiver. We also explore the geometric structure of the black hole moduli space, including its metric and entropy function.

We introduce a novel class of reward-predictive state representations (R-PSRs) designed to model partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). These representations extend prior work on state representations by enabling the prediction of future rewards within a single linear prediction, a capability that traditional PSRs lack. We demonstrate that R-PSRs offer a distinct advantage: they allow for the exact computation of optimal policies and their corresponding values through standard dynamic programming. Furthermore, we establish that R-PSRs are applicable to a strictly broader range of POMDPs than standard PSRs. We validate the utility of R-PSRs by applying them to a suite of POMDP test cases, including scenarios where the method successfully derives optimal policies and values.

Gentrification-induced displacement remains a significant challenge for policymakers, yet early warning systems could assist in tackling this issue. This study introduces a novel approach for forecasting gentrification by integrating graph neural networks (GNNs) with spatio-temporal data. We developed a graph convolutional autoencoder (GCA) to learn a low-dimensional representation of the input graph, which is then projected onto a grid to create a spatio-temporal graph. This structure is subsequently processed by a GNN to generate predictions. We evaluated this framework using a real-world dataset of U.S. housing prices and demonstrated its efficacy through a comparison with baseline models.

This study investigates the magnetic phase diagram of a thin film of the compound Mn$_2$Au, which exhibits a complex interplay between spin-orbit coupling and magnetocrystalline anisotropy. Utilizing a phenomenological model that incorporates both anisotropy and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions, we analyze the field-induced phase diagram along the [110] direction. Our results indicate that the field-driven sequence of transitions is consistent with experimental observations. Specifically, we observe a metastable skyrmion lattice that evolves into a stable hexagonal magnetic phase as the applied field becomes increasingly negative. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the energy barrier separating the skyrmion lattice and the hexagonal phase is highly sensitive to the magnitude of the anisotropy.

This paper demonstrates that certain isometric composition operators defined on harmonic Bloch-type spaces must be trivial. Additionally, we provide specific representations for such operators that are simultaneously bimathematically and algebraically equivalent to isometric composition operators acting within harmonic Besov spaces.

This study examines the deployment of range-extended vehicles (REVs) within urban delivery routing contexts. We present a novel mixed-integer linear programming framework designed to jointly optimize delivery routes and charging station locations. The objective is to minimize operational expenses while adhering to a vehicle energy budget, thereby reducing both vehicle miles traveled (miles) and the frequency of intermediate charges. The analysis utilizes a case study of a delivery network in New York City, incorporating real-world road networks and charging infrastructure. The results indicate that integrating REVs can lower energy costs and vehicle miles, though this requires more charging stops. Furthermore, we identify that the optimal placement of charging stations is sensitive to the count of available REVs, the specific charging locations, and the spatial distribution of deliveries.

The Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) is utilized to determine the leptonic decay constants of light pseudoscalar mesons, a task that is typically intricate due to the rigorous dependence on the four-momentum. However, this complexity is alleviated by applying the Feynman-Källén-Lehmann (FKL) spectral representation to the BSE kernel. This approach transforms the original four-dimensional integral into a manageable one-dimensional integral, which is subsequently solved using the Gauss-Laguerre quadrature method.

This study examines the error estimation for the finite element approximation of transient Stokes equations. We demonstrate that applying the backward Euler or Crank-Nicolson schemes for temporal discretization, coupled with the Croucet (or similar) method for spatial problems, leads to the optimal error estimates in the $L^2(0,T;H)$ and $L^2(0,T;H)$ norms. Furthermore, we derive optimal error estimates in the $L^2(0,T;H)$ and $L^\infty(0,T;H)$ norms for the Crank-Nicolson scheme when applied to the Stokes equations. We introduce a visualization system designed to offer a comprehensive view of a machine learning model's performance in detecting objects within autonomous driving contexts. This system enables users to examine performance across various locations and times, highlighting areas where the model struggles. By integrating geo-aware data visualization, it establishes a direct link between model accuracy and environmental factors, thereby supporting targeted dataset expansion and improving the model's overall robustness. Furthermore, the tool includes a feature for comparing the performance of multiple models, allowing analysts to pinpoint specific regions where one model outperforms another.

This study investigates the photoresponse characteristics of GaN metal-semiconductor field-effect transistors (MESFETs) by integrating a two-dimensional (2D) drift-diffusion model with a two-band Monte Carlo simulation. The Monte Carlo approach calculates carrier transport and optical absorption within the channel, while the 2D model handles photoionization effects trapped within the gate dielectric and their subsequent influence on drain current. Results indicate that drain current is enhanced by the photoionization of both electrons and holes trapped in the gate oxide. Furthermore, a gate-length-dependent reduction in the photocurrent is observed, attributed to a decline in trapped charge density within the gate region as the gate length decreases.

This study introduces a novel approach to vehicle navigation that integrates a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) with a Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) system. The proposed method enhances positioning accuracy by leveraging a GMM to estimate the vehicle's position relative to the map. The system relies on a dataset comprising 100 kilometers of driving data collected in the United States, which includes both road and off-road segments. Experimental results demonstrate that the GMM-based vehicle positioning significantly outperforms a standard SLAM implementation, achieving a mean absolute error of 0.32 meters compared to 0.5 meters for SLAM alone.

We present SG-PALM, a scalable framework for unsupervised pre-training of language models. SG-PALM achieves scalability by employing stochastic gradient descent to minimize a loss function that aggregates contributions from multiple data samples. This approach enables the efficient training of a 7B-parameter model on 1,024 NVIDIA A100 GPUs using 53 terabytes of text data, with a total training duration of 5.5 hours. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method yields superior performance compared to various supervised fine-tuning techniques, including supervised fine-tuning, in zero-shot and few-shot evaluation settings.

This paper presents a methodology for regulating the frequency of falling objects by integrating a standard PID controller with a randomized, variable-speed release mechanism. The approach is demonstrated through a case study involving a ball drop system, where a solenoid valve modulates its opening duration to create a controlled degree of randomness in release times. Solenoid operation is governed by a PID controller that adjusts the probability of a drop based on the discrepancy between the measured and target frequencies. The resulting system is characterized by its inherent stochasticity, making it an ideal candidate for a study in statistical control. Furthermore, the research explores the system's long-term behavior and its performance across various parameter settings.

This study explores user scheduling and power distribution within cache-enabled wireless networks employing network coding. We introduce a novel coding scheme that leverages cached content to facilitate user scheduling and power allocation, thereby reducing the transmission power required by the base station. Our approach relies on the premise that network coding is accessible for a pair of users, allowing the base station to transmit a combined signal at a single power level, which both users can decode. We formulate an optimization problem aimed at maximizing the system's minimum data rate while adhering to power and cache size limits. To tackle this, we develop an iterative algorithm comprising two stages: first, a joint optimization of user scheduling and cache placement, followed by power allocation. The algorithm's convergence is proven, and numerical simulations confirm that the proposed scheme outperforms traditional methods lacking network coding.

The PPT square conjecture has been resolved in the negative for all dimensions up to 9, with the highest known dimension where counterexamples occur being 10. This document introduces a streamlined method for constructing such counterexamples in the odd square dimensions 10 and 18, utilizing the theory of PPT spaces.

This study examines $G;C$, an Abelian group defined by inverse-closed generating sets, and investigates the subgroup $\Phi(G;C)$, which serves as its analogue to the Frattini subgroup. We establish that for any such group $G;C$, the equality $\Phi(G;C) = \bigcap \{ M \leq G;C \text{ is maximal} \}$ holds. Furthermore, we derive several foundational properties of $G;C$, including a criterion for determining whether it is cyclic.

This study examines Time-of-Arrival (ToA)-based localization within a 2D environment, specifically addressing the non-linear nature of the underlying equations. The primary objective is to determine the optimal placement of anchors and estimate target positions using these equations. The analysis begins by establishing the fundamental constraints governing anchor placement, revealing that reliable positioning outside the convex hull formed by the anchors is unattainable. Subsequently, an optimization framework is introduced to identify the best anchor locations, with the solution derived via a specialized algorithm. The method's performance is validated through simulations, which demonstrate a significant reduction in root mean square error (RMSE) compared to existing anchor placement strategies.

This study examines the shear modulus of light elements—hydrogen, helium, and lithium—under extreme pressures, utilizing a pressure- and temperature-dependent equation of state derived from density functional theory (DFT) calculations. The analysis reveals that the shear modulus for these elements initially rises with pressure up to approximately $10^7$ g/cm$^3$, after which it decreases. This behavior is attributed to the transition from a shear-stable regime to a shear-unstable regime, a shift driven by the evolution of the electronic band structure. The findings suggest that the shear-unstable state is likely to be the stable phase within the interiors of giant planets.

This study introduces a new framework for deblurring images corrupted by motion blur. We propose a reblurring module that generates synthetic blur kernels to produce a reblurred image, which serves as an enhanced intermediate target for the main learning process. By creating a reblurred target with a higher contrast between the sharp and blurred regions, the network can more effectively learn the mapping from blurred to sharp images. To further improve the quality of the intermediate reblurred image, we incorporate a residual connection that helps the network retain details from the original input. Additionally, a new loss function is designed to penalize the discrepancy between the final network output and the proposed intermediate target. Experiments demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on standard benchmarks.

Tidal disruption events (TDEs) are rare galactic nuclear outbursts caused by the disruption of stars by supermassive black holes. This study presents a new TDE candidate, AT2020mno, which was identified in the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) survey. The event is located in the galaxy NGC 4649 at a redshift of $z=0.014$ and exhibits a host luminosity of $L_{\rm host} = 10^{10.6} L_{\odot}$. Its optical light curve displays a rapid rise and a slow decline, with a peak luminosity of $L_{\rm peak} = 10^{42.2} L_{\odot}$, indicating a black hole mass of $M_{\rm BH} = 10^{6.5} M_{\odot}$. The peak emission is dominated by the Balmer series, with a spectral index of $\beta = 0.5$, and the broad H$\beta$ line has a full width at half maximum of 10,000 km/s. These characteristics—specifically the spectral index and line width—distinguish AT2020mno from active galactic nuclei and supernovae. We present a comprehensive analysis of Lyα emitters (LAEs) at redshifts $z \sim 6.5–7.0$ using the Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC) survey. By combining HSC data with Subaru UV continuum observations, we identified 1,000 LAE candidates, which were then cross-matched with the COSMOS 3D catalog to determine their three-dimensional spatial distribution. Our findings reveal that LAE candidates are preferentially located in the vicinity of massive galaxy clusters and filaments, indicating a strong correlation between LAE density and the underlying cosmic web structure. Furthermore, we observed a significant increase in the number of LAEs in the regions of the COSMOS 3D catalog that exhibit the highest overdensities. These results suggest that LAEs are highly effective tracers for studying galaxy formation in the early universe.

This study examines the cold dwell behavior of Ti-6Al alloys, focusing on the interplay between the applied stress and the grain boundary temperature. The research highlights that the stress difference at grain boundaries reaches its peak at approximately 400 K, a finding that aligns with the peak in the temperature-dependent coefficient of the grain boundary diffusivity.

Feature Model solvers are essential for automatically verifying the existence of valid configurations in feature models. However, these models can become computationally infeasible when they include numerous features and complex, nested cross-tree constraints. This paper introduces a novel method for enhancing solver efficiency by partitioning the model into smaller, independent components that can be processed in parallel. Our approach identifies a minimal set of "hubs"—features heavily connected to numerous constraints—and assigns them as root nodes to separate the model into distinct trees. These trees are then distributed across a multi-core environment for concurrent processing. Our experimental results indicate that accuracy depends on the volume of features and cross-tree constraints, with higher feature counts and constraint counts generally yielding better outcomes. Furthermore, we observed that increasing the number of available parallel cores significantly improves performance.

We introduce a new pipeline designed to identify faint companions to nearby stars, utilizing the 10-meter Keck I telescope and the Near-Infrared Imaging Camera (NIRC2) at the Keck Observatory. The system employs a dual-camera approach: a coronagraphic imager for high-contrast imaging and a standard camera for reference images. This setup enables the detection of companions down to a mass of approximately 10 Jupiter masses ($10 M_J$) at separations of roughly 0.5 arcseconds, a sensitivity level exceeding the planet-mass threshold of the original GPI Coronagraphic Survey. We applied this pipeline to 10 nearby stars, including 9 previously studied by the GPI Survey and one additional target. Our results confirm the detection of companions to 10 of the 10 observed stars, with 9 of these being brown dwarfs. Notably, we discovered a new brown dwarf companion to the star HD 161694, which had been missed by the earlier survey. Furthermore, our pipeline successfully detects brown dwarfs at mass limits about 10 times lower than GPI, demonstrating its efficacy in finding brown dwarfs at separations of roughly 0.5 arcseconds.

This study examines the equilibrium state of a two-dimensional system comprising two distinct charges, $q_1$ and $q_2$, situated within a plasma. The analysis focuses on two scenarios: one where symmetry remains unbroken and another where it is explicitly broken. In the unbroken case, charges conserve their total sum, $q_1 + q_2 = Q$, whereas in the broken case, they are fixed individually as $q_1$ and $q_2$. The findings indicate that for unbroken symmetry, the probability distribution of $Q$ follows a Gaussian profile, whereas under explicit symmetry breaking, the distribution of individual charges exhibits a non-Gaussian shape.

We introduce a quantum simulator utilizing a one-dimensional Bose-Hubbard model to emulate both Chern insulators and Weyl semimetals. This setup enables the investigation of the phase transition connecting these two states, specifically by adjusting the model parameters. Furthermore, we utilize the system's topological invariants to distinguish between the resulting phases.

We introduce a novel approach to predicting future frames in video sequences. Unlike previous methods that rely on high-level supervision, our model learns by minimizing the difference between generated predictions and the ground truth. The architecture consists of two components: a recurrent neural network that processes past frames to forecast the next one, and a refinement network that adjusts this initial forecast using features from subsequent available frames. The latter is guided by a lightweight auxiliary predictor that estimates the direction of motion between the future time steps. This auxiliary predictor is trained to align with actual ground truth motion, enabling the refinement network to be trained entirely through self-supervision. The network's primary loss function is the mean squared error between the final refined output and the real future frame. We validate our method on the Kinetics-400 dataset, demonstrating that it achieves state-of-the-art performance in predicting future frames.

Mitochondrial diseases are prevalent and often fatal, with heteroplasmy variance—referring to the proportion of mutant versus wild-type mitochondria—playing a critical role in determining tissue health. Although current methods for quantifying heteroplasmy are accurate, they are labor-intensive and demand extensive sequencing. To address this, we developed a novel, rapid, and cost-effective approach that leverages the specific properties of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and its unique structure. This new method utilizes a single PCR reaction combined with a single sequencing run to simultaneously determine both the quantity of mtDNA and the precise level of heteroplasmy. We successfully applied this technique to analyze cells derived from patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and human fibroblasts. Furthermore, we demonstrated its utility in monitoring mtDNA levels and heteroplasmy shifts during mitochondrial disease therapies. Ultimately, this streamlined methodology offers a practical solution for investigating the pathophysiology of mitochondrial diseases and evaluating therapeutic interventions.

This study introduces a novel text-to-speech framework, Mixer-TTS, which employs a Mixer-based architecture to generate speech from text. The proposed model utilizes a U-Net structure, where both the encoder and decoder are populated with Mixer blocks. These blocks leverage attention mechanisms across sequences to capture extensive long-range contextual information. Experimental results indicate that Mixer-TTS produces outputs with MOS scores that are comparable to, and in some cases exceed, those of the original LJSpeech recordings. Furthermore, the system demonstrates superior performance in both speech quality and the preservation of prosody compared to existing models.
